LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Notice, Name, Share Feelings & Ask for Help — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson condenses the whole class into one habit: the check-in — four steps that turn a storm inside into a sentence outside.

What is this?

Notice, name, share feelings and ask for help are the four steps of the check-in: notice what is happening inside, name the feeling, share it out loud and — when it is too big to carry alone — call for help.

What does it mean?

A feeling that gets noticed, named and shared almost never has to come out as a tantrum. The check-in is not one skill among many — it is the delivery system that carries every other word of this class to where it is needed.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: feelings announce themselves in the BODY first (chest, tummy, hot face) — the noticing is a body scan; the naming can start fuzzy ("something big") and sharpen later; and ask-for-help is not the last resort — it is step four of the design.

Why this matters

This is the engine card of the class: every feeling word learned so far rides on the check-in. Children who run these four steps daily need fewer meltdowns, recover faster and ask for help sooner — the trifecta.

What it teaches

Interoception (reading internal signals), emotion labelling under real conditions, self-disclosure (sharing is a social skill too), and help-seeking — the skill teachers and parents wish every child had installed.

Words to learn

noticenameshare feelingsask for helpcheck-inweather insidetoo big

Say this to your child

“"Here is the check-in — the strongest habit on the whole feelings path. Step one, NOTICE: put a hand on your chest and ask, what is happening inside? Something is always happening. Step two, NAME it: start fuzzy — something big — then try names until one fits: worried? frustrated? excited? Step three, SHARE it: say it out loud to someone safe — I feel worried. Step four, the safety net: if the feeling is too big to carry alone, ASK FOR HELP — can you help me? That is not giving up. That is exactly what step four is for. Four steps, two minutes, and the storm has somewhere to go."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The check-in — four steps from storm to sentence."
  2. Read the panels: the hand-raised boy NOTICES, the chin-finger girl NAMEs IT, the open-hand boy SHAREs FEELINGS, the clasped-hands girl is ready to ASK FOR HELP.
  3. Run the body scan: close eyes, one breath, "where do you feel something? Chest? Tummy? Face?" — noticing is scanning, not guessing.
  4. Practise the fuzzy-to-sharp move: "something big… is it angry? worried? excited? — let us try names until one fits."
  5. Close with the daily ritual below and the takeaway: "notice, name, share — and the fourth step is always there: ask for help."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels run the check-in: Notice Feelings, a boy with his hand raised mid-notice; Name It, a girl with a finger to her chin; Share Feelings, a boy telling with an open hand; and Ask for Help, a girl with hands clasped, ready to ask — the delivery system of the whole class, in four frames.

Ask your child

"Where do you feel feelings in your body?" "What if the name will not come — can we start fuzzy?" "What do we do when the feeling is too big?" "Who are your help-people?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My tummy feels something big!" "I feel worried" (the whole system, working) or the request: "can you help me with my big feeling?"

Out in the real world

Check-in weather happens twice a day at minimum: breakfast ("what is the weather inside this morning?") and bedtime ("what was the biggest feeling today?"). Build the ritual at those two anchors and the steps carry themselves — storms get reported in sentences by the second week.

Try it together

The Feelings Weather Report: a pretend microphone, and everyone takes turns broadcasting their inside weather — "this morning in my chest: cloudy with a chance of grumpy, clearing after breakfast." Grown-ups go first with a real one. The child’s forecast may be silly; the noticing underneath it is not. Two minutes, twice a day, habit installed.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the check-in start — the body or the mouth? What if the name will not come? What is step four?" Body, start fuzzy, ask for help — three answers and the check-in is running.

Parent tips

Accept fuzzy names happily — "a big something" is a valid step two; precision arrives with practice. And make the help-people explicit: name three (and include one outside the house — a teacher, a grandparent), because a child who knows exactly WHO to ask asks sooner. Ask-for-help praised loudly is a meltdowns-later investment.

This lesson pairs with the Notice, Name, Share Feelings & Ask for Help flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
